topic: LLM annotator performance on non-English languages
hypothesis_a: GPT-3 shows meaningful potential as a data annotator even on languages other than English, suggesting its effectiveness as an annotator extends beyond English-only settings.
hypothesis_b: Open-source LLMs show a considerable decline in performance when applied to non-English languages (evaluated on French, Dutch, and English NLI tasks), indicating current open-source models do not generalize well as annotators outside English.

hypothesis_a: Effective discrete prompts can be discovered via task-agnostic reinforcement learning, learning a general prompt-optimization policy rather than adapting the prompt to each individual query.
hypothesis_b: Effective prompting instead requires test-time, query-dependent reinforcement learning that evaluates and adapts the prompt separately for each specific input, rather than relying on one fixed task-agnostic policy.

topic: distributional acquisition of syntactic categories in children
hypothesis_a: The child represents each target word as a context vector of frequently co-occurring words, then iteratively groups words into categories using a similarity score computed over these vectors.
hypothesis_b: The child does not need vector-based similarity computations; it is sufficient for the child to count how often words occur within particular frames and group together the words that appear in the most frequent frames.

topic: nature of language: symbol system vs. use
hypothesis_a: Language, like cognition generally, can be defined as an abstract, formal symbol-manipulation system, in line with computational theories of mind.
hypothesis_b: Language is not an abstract symbol-manipulation system; it is a system that has a function and acquires meaning only when it is actually used to do things in the world.

hypothesis_a: LLMs can iteratively improve their own outputs through self-refinement, using self-generated feedback to critique and revise their own responses without external input.
hypothesis_b: LLMs cannot reliably self-correct their own reasoning errors; without external feedback, self-correction attempts fail to fix, and can even worsen, their initial responses.

topic: mechanistic view of transformer feed-forward layers
hypothesis_a: Transformer feed-forward layers function as key-value memories at the level of individual neurons: each neuron/key correlates with a textual pattern in the training data, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary.
hypothesis_b: Based on causal tracing analysis of GPT-2, transformer MLP layers are better characterized as a single linear associative memory rather than a collection of per-neuron key-value pairs.

hypothesis_a: Lexical overlap between source and target languages is a highly important feature for predicting cross-lingual transfer success on syntactic tasks (POS tagging, NER, dependency parsing), but a much less important feature for the semantic task of NLI.
hypothesis_b: Lexical overlap shows the opposite importance pattern across task types when predicting zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance, contrary to the syntactic-vs-semantic pattern found elsewhere.
